name: Tamoxifen
lead: Tamoxifen, sold under the brand name Nolvadex among others, is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) taken by mouth. It acts as an oestrogen antagonist in breast tissue and as an agonist in some other tissues.[1][2] The US label (for the oral solution Soltamox) lists treatment of metastatic breast cancer, adjuvant treatment of early-stage ER-positive breast cancer, reduction of risk after DCIS surgery, and risk reduction in high-risk women.[3]

In appearance and bodybuilding settings it is used off-label, mostly to address gynecomastia and to manage oestrogen effects during or after anabolic steroid use.[4][5][6] Looksmax.org users also ask whether SERMs affect growth-plate closure, with threads citing conflicting laboratory findings.[8]
The US label carries a boxed warning for uterine malignancies, stroke and pulmonary embolism in the oncology setting, and warns of fetal harm and liver effects.[3] It is a prescription medicine.
infobox: UK 1973, US 1977 for advanced breast cancer (per Grokipedia)

paras: The label's approved indications are summarised above.[3] The 2015 patient-level meta-analysis of aromatase inhibitors versus tamoxifen, the SOFT and TEXT trials of tamoxifen with ovarian suppression in premenopausal women, and low-dose tamoxifen trials in breast intraepithelial neoplasia are among the large bodies of evidence.[9][10][11][12][13] An earlier systematic review examined adjuvant and neoadjuvant breast cancer treatments' effects on mortality.[14] Grokipedia describes off-label use in male infertility and gynecomastia.[1]

Gynecomastia is the chief appearance-related use. A looksmax.org user says they took tamoxifen for 20 days for gynecomastia, reported excess sweating only, and said it helped muscle gain; another says their gynecomastia hurts and hopes tamoxifen will resolve it.[4][5] A review on anabolic-steroid-induced hypogonadism lists selective oestrogen receptor modulators among management options for men with a history of non-prescribed steroid use.[6]

The boxed warning cites uterine malignancies (endometrial adenocarcinoma 2.20 versus 0.71 per 1,000 woman-years on placebo in the NSABP P-1 trial), stroke and pulmonary embolism, with fatal cases.[3] The label lists hot flashes, mood disturbances, vaginal discharge and bleeding, nausea and fluid retention as common reactions, plus embryo-fetal toxicity and liver cancer and abnormalities, some fatal.[3] Case literature describes tamoxifen retinopathy and thrombocytopenia.[15][16][17] These data come mainly from women treated for breast cancer; Grokipedia notes that thromboembolic risk has also been described in men.[1]

Tamoxifen is an oestrogen agonist/antagonist that competes with oestrogen for the oestrogen receptor, decreasing receptor-dependent growth signalling in breast tissue.[3] Grokipedia describes agonist activity in bone and endometrium.[2] Laboratory research has compared oestrogen receptor alpha and beta binding specificity.[18]

Grokipedia reports that tamoxifen was developed at Imperial Chemical Industries in the late 1950s and early 1960s as a potential morning-after contraceptive, failed in that role, and was repurposed for breast cancer; it was approved in the UK in 1973 and the US in 1977, and the FDA added chemoprevention in 1998 based on the NSABP P-1 trial.[1] The P-1 prevention study was published in 1998.[19]

Evidence in humans is chiefly in breast cancer: P-1 prevention,[19] the Early Breast Cancer Trialists' overview,[23] aromatase inhibitor comparisons,[9] SOFT/TEXT,[10][11][12] and low-dose TAM-01.[13][20] Registered studies cover other cancers, ovulation induction with clomiphene plus tamoxifen, and hepatitis C.[21][22]

No randomised trial of tamoxifen for gynecomastia in bodybuilders or for growth-plate effects in healthy adolescents was identified; the forum thread on growth plates cites laboratory studies with conflicting conclusions.[8]

On looksmax.org tamoxifen (Nolvadex) is discussed with testosterone and in gynecomastia threads.[4][5] A growth-plate thread quotes a cultured-bone study finding dose-dependent growth retardation and an in vivo study reporting that tamoxifen stimulated longitudinal growth in contrast to oestradiol; a reply says SERMs have mild oestrogenic effects on bone and advises against using them for that purpose without endocrinology expertise.[8]

lore.intro: Tamoxifen appears in gynecomastia and steroid-aftercare discussion and, less often, in questions about growth plates.[4][5][8]

claims.believers: Users report using it for gynecomastia and say pain or swelling improves.[4][5]
claims.experts: Gynecomastia is not among the label indications, and no controlled trial in bodybuilders was found in the sources reviewed.[3]

claims.claim: Tamoxifen helps muscle gain by blocking oestrogen
claims.believers: A user reports faster muscle gain while on it.[4]
claims.experts: No controlled data in this setting were found in the sources reviewed.

claims.claim: SERMs like Nolvadex affect growth-plate closure
claims.believers: A poster compiles laboratory studies with opposite findings on tamoxifen and bone growth.[8]
claims.experts: No human trial in healthy adolescents was found; tamoxifen acts as an agonist or antagonist depending on tissue.[2]

card.summary: A breast-cancer SERM that bodybuilders and TRT users take for gynecomastia; label carries a boxed warning and nothing tests it for looks.
card.note: Boxed warning for uterine cancers, stroke and pulmonary embolism; appearance uses are off-label.

quick.overview:
Tamoxifen (Nolvadex) is a prescription oestrogen-receptor blocker for breast cancer. In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding circles it is used off-label for gynecomastia and oestrogen control during steroid use, and some ask about growth-plate effects.

A review says it has been tried successfully in adolescent gynecomastia; no trials address its other cosmetic uses.
quick.mechanism: It binds oestrogen receptors, blocking oestrogen's effect in breast tissue while acting like oestrogen in other tissues such as bone and endometrium.
quick.risks: The US label's boxed warning covers uterine cancers, stroke and pulmonary embolism; it also lists liver effects, hot flashes and fetal harm. Retinopathy and low platelets have been reported. Prescription-only.
